extracted.intended_audience: second-language teachers, SLA researchers, and teacher-educators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and theoretical criteria for designing classroom activities and interventions that harness emotion (especially positive-broadening emotion) and imagination (possible selves) to facilitate second-language learning. Includes diagnostic, intervention, and design principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multidimensional definition of emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions are short-lived, feeling-arousal-purposive-expressive phenomena that help us adapt to opportunities and challenges (Reeve, 2005).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a multidimensional lens when analyzing emotion: (a) feeling = subjective experience; (b) arousal = physiological responses; (c) purposive = goal-directedness; (d) expressive = social/communicative signals. Treat emotion as emergent from coordination of these aspects rather than any single component.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish emotion from mood and temperament
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotions are short-lived and action-oriented; moods are longer-lasting, diffuse background states; temperament is a stable disposition that biases emotional/mood tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing interventions or interpreting learner behaviour, differentiate whether you're targeting momentary emotional reactions (e.g., anxiety in class), longer-term moods that shape daily functioning, or trait dispositions (e.g., trait anxiety, optimism) that require different pedagogical responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-order emotions versus higher-order emotion schemas
rubrics_metrics.description: First-order emotions are fast, perceptual or imaging-triggered responses (interest, joy, fear, etc.). Higher-order emotion schemas involve interactions between feelings and higher cognition (thoughts, strategies, goals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect adults to primarily experience complex emotion schemas and vibes shaped by cognition; interventions may therefore need cognitive components (e.g., reappraisal, imagery, self-regulation) to alter emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-dimension conceptualization: positive-broadening and negative-narrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional experience is usefully conceptualized along two separate dimensions: positive-broadening (promotes exploration, resource-building) and negative-narrowing (promotes focused, avoidance-oriented responses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess learners on both axes rather than as opposites; recognize ambivalence (co-occurrence) and design activities that modulate each dimension appropriately depending on instructional goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden-and-build functions of positive emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Positive emotions broaden momentary thought–action repertoires and build enduring personal resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fredrickson's five functions to consider: (1) broaden attention and thinking → exploration/play/new learning; (2) undo lingering effects of negative arousal; (3) promote resilience and recovery under stress; (4) build physical/intellectual/social/psychological resources; (5) contribute to upward spirals toward well-being. Use activities that intentionally create these outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific tendencies of positive emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Fredrickson lists tendencies linked to particular positive emotions: joy → play/creativity; interest → exploration/absorption; contentment → savoring/integration; pride → sharing/imagining future achievements; love → sustained meaningful relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select or design classroom tasks to evoke these particular positive emotions depending on desired learning outcomes (e.g., creative tasks to evoke joy, cultural exploration to evoke interest).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory vs anticipated emotions
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipatory emotions are currently experienced reactions to the prospect of a future event (e.g., hope, fear). Anticipated emotions are imagined emotions that one expects to feel in the future after an event occurs (e.g., anticipated joy or regret).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both kinds to motivate learners: provoke helpful anticipatory emotions (hope) in the present and guide learners to vividly imagine anticipated positive feelings associated with successful L2 outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of imagination/possible selves to provoke emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible selves are vivid, specific representations of future self-states (ideal self, feared self) that act as personalized carriers of goals and aspirations and can arouse emotional reactions that motivate behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have learners create vivid, detailed images of their ideal and feared L2 selves; connect those images to actionable plans so the emotion provoked translates into sustained effort rather than mere fantasy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dörnyei's L2 self system: three dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The L2 self system comprises (1) the ideal L2 self (the future vision of who the learner wants to become), (2) the ought-to self (duties/obligations shaped by external expectations), and (3) the L2 learning experience (present learning environment factors such as teacher, curriculum, peers, and past successes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design activities that link progress in language to learners' ideal and ought-to selves while optimizing present L2 learning experience variables to support ongoing motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 1 for motivating possible selves: vividness and elaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The ease of creating an effective possible ideal self varies; once established, a self-image must be elaborate and vivid to act as an effective motivator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use guided imagery, visual prompts, storytelling, or multimedia to increase vividness; scaffold elaboration with questions that elicit sensory, contextual, and action details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 2: perceived attainability
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible selves only have value when the creator believes their attainment is possible and likely; they are not just fantasy or vague wishes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground visions in realistic milestones, show examples/models of attainable progress, and provide evidence and small wins to strengthen perceived attainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 3: internal consistency (harmony between ideal and ought-to selves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Harmony between the ideal and ought-to selves (alignment of social and personal identities) increases the efficacy of possible selves as motivators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitate reflection on personal and social identities, help reconcile external obligations with personal aspirations, and adjust goals to reduce conflict when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 4: activation in working memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Activation of the possible self in working memory can be prompted by reminders, classroom exercises, and self-relevant actions, or learners can be taught to purposefully summon possible selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use frequent reminders, classroom routines, imagery exercises, prompts, and cues (posters, journal prompts, goal-checklists) to keep possible selves salient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 5: procedural strategies accompany imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: To move from potential to action, learners must have accompanying procedural strategies (imagery + inventory of applicable plans and procedures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach concrete action plans, step-by-step strategies, and self-monitoring techniques alongside imagery-based motivation; ensure plans are reviewed and updated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition 6: balance with feared/feared-self (ambivalence)
rubrics_metrics.description: For optimal motivational effectiveness, ideal and ought-to selves need to be offset by the impact of the feared self; balance maximizes motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage learners to consider potential negative outcomes as part of planning (activate 'dreaded' selves occasionally) to create appropriate urgency without debilitating anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy 1: raise awareness of the construction of the ideal L2 self
rubrics_metrics.description: Help learners become conscious of their existing aspirations and guide selection from those multiple possible selves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflection activities, interviews, and guided discussions to elicit prior imaginings and encourage selection of motivating future selves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy 2: imagery enhancement
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengthen the vision of possible selves through guided or creative imagery to boost controllability and vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement guided imagery sessions, visualization scripts, role-play of future scenarios, and sensory detail elicitation exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy 3: make the ideal L2 self plausible (substantiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase motivation by making the ideal L2 self believable through realistic expectations and supporting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of attainable success, set incremental goals, teach necessary skills, and connect vision to concrete milestones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy 4: keep the vision alive through activation
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain engagement by providing an engaging framework that keeps the enthusiastic engaged and less-enthusiastic thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ongoing activation: reminders, engaging projects, regular imagery refreshers, peer sharing, and classroom rituals that reference future selves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy 5: develop an action plan and ongoing planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Help learners operationalize visions with concrete action plans and continuous self-evaluation; revise ineffective plans and celebrate success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach planning skills, milestone setting, self-monitoring tools (logs, checklists), and schedule regular reviews and celebrations of progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy 6: counterbalance positive vision by highlighting costs of failure
rubrics_metrics.description: For optimal motivation, occasionally activate feared selves to highlight potential consequences of inaction, balancing hope with realistic tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflective prompts about losses associated with not achieving goals, but avoid inducing debilitating anxiety; balance with relaxation and coping strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic desensitization as a three-step process
rubrics_metrics.description: A counter-conditioning approach to reduce intensity of negative-narrowing emotional responses (language anxiety): (a) construct hierarchy chart; (b) relaxation training; (c) desensitization sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implement in sequence: build individualized hierarchy of anxieties, teach relaxation until learner can relax in 3–4 minutes, then repeatedly imagine hierarchy items while relaxed until anxiety dissipates before moving to next item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct anxiety hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners create an individualized list of language-learning situations ordered from least to most anxiety-provoking (most powerful triggers at the bottom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete classroom triggers (e.g., fill-in-the-blank, journal writing, speaking to native speaker, oral exams, public presentations). Use the hierarchy to structure graded exposure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation training: physiological/cognitive/affective/social benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Relaxation reduces physiological arousal, improves concentration, reduces frustration, boosts confidence, and yields more socially paced communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach learners that relaxation prepares them for exposure; measure readiness by learner's ability to relax in ~3–4 minutes; incorporate respiratory control, progressive slowdown of heart/breathing, and muscle tension awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relaxation techniques: autogenic, progressive muscle relaxation, visualization
rubrics_metrics.description: Three recommended techniques: (a) Autogenic (self-suggestions, body awareness, controlled breathing); (b) Progressive muscle relaxation (tensing and relaxing muscle groups); (c) Visualization (guided sensory-rich journeys to calming places).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model techniques, have learners practice and choose the most effective one, and integrate preferred method into desensitization sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desensitization sessions: imaginal graded exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Learners vividly imagine hierarchy items in detail while completely relaxed; repeat until the imagined scenario no longer elicits anxiety, then progress to next item.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated imaginal exposure before in-vivo practice; ensure relaxation is achieved first; only move up the hierarchy when the learner can imagine the item without anxiety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance guideline: positivity ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Fredrickson & Losada suggest that well-functioning persons have between 3 and 11 positive emotions to each negative one; use as a rough guide for balancing positive-broadening and negative-narrowing emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim pedagogical climates toward substantially more positive experiences than negative ones, while accounting for individual temperament (optimist/pessimist differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher immediacy and approach behaviors
rubrics_metrics.description: Teacher immediacy (reducing psychological distance) includes nonlinguistic behaviors (reduced physical distance, relaxed postures, gestures, smiling, vocal variety, eye contact) and language behaviors (personal examples, questions, humor, addressing by name, praise, inclusive pronouns).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use immediacy to foster affiliation and stimulate positive-broadening emotions; combine with appropriate task choices to build positive classroom atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage play and exploration to broaden mindsets
rubrics_metrics.description: Play and exploration promote discovery of novel/creative actions, ideas, and social bonds, fostering the positive-broadening tendencies (joy, interest, contentment, pride, love).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design playful, exploratory tasks that invite creative risk-taking, experimentation, and collaborative discovery to enhance learning and resource-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop resilience through teachable strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Resiliency helps recover from stress; strengths like humor, creative exploration, relaxation, and optimistic thinking can be taught and tailored to L2 contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model resilient behaviours, teach coping strategies, integrate humor and optimism training, and select activities that build adaptive coping and faster recovery from setbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foster community-level positive emotion and avoid negative climates
rubrics_metrics.description: Resilient individuals cultivate positive emotions and elicit them in others; teachers should build supportive social contexts and avoid negativity, sarcasm, disapproval, and cynicism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inquiry language to explore positions, advocacy language to support peers, praise, and inclusive interaction formats to create flourishing groups that reinforce individual resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two general approaches to influencing student emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers can (a) set up conditions to provoke emotional reactions, and (b) work with cognition that modifies the emotional schema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine situational design (tasks, reminders, imagery) with cognitive interventions (reappraisal, planning, relaxation) to both evoke desired emotions and reshape how learners interpret and regulate them.
